en: The *Śramaṇa-fǎbǎo-zhuàn-lùn* states:

As for what was mentioned above regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the following twenty verses provide a detailed explanation of the five aggregates, as well as their classification into bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*). This section consists of thirteen sub-divisions.
It consists of four sections.
The first five and a half verses clarify the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha),
as well as its divisions into bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu).
The passage consists of five parts.
The first half-verse enumerates the eleven types of matter in general;
the second half-verse distinguishes the five sense organs (*indriya*).
The third section, consisting of one verse, analyzes the five types of objective form (*rūpa-viṣaya*).
The fourth section, consisting of three verses, analyzes non-informative form (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
The fifth section, consisting of half a verse, classifies the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) by way of bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*); this is the first [of those].
The verse says: "Reaching and non-informative [matter].
Next, the verse is cited as the answer.
The treatise says: "[From] 'reaching' up to the establishment of the name 'aggregate of matter' (rūpaskandha)."
This is an explanation of the verse.
It may be understood according to the text.
Treatise.
Among these, the characteristics of the five faculties should first be explained.
The second half-verse distinguishes the characteristics of the five faculties.
The Commentary says: "Regarding the five faculties, beginning with the eye..."
This is the commentary on the verse. Regarding that "consciousness," there are two interpretations:
first, it refers to the consciousness of form and so forth; second, it refers to—
Regarding those consciousnesses of the eye and so forth,
this first passage states that the basis for the consciousness of form is called the eye-faculty,
and so on up to...
The basis for contact-consciousness is called the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).
The treatise states:
"As the Blessed One has said," up to the full exposition as follows.
This citation from the Sūtra proves that the five faculties are translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*).
The Treatise says:
"Alternatively, 'those' refers to nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness."
This is the second explanation:
that consciousness is named after its sense organ (*indriya*).
[From the] Treatise.
The meaning of that consciousness’s basis, up to its point of reliance,
is as follows: the basis of visual consciousness is called the eye-faculty,
and so on, up to...
That which is the support for body-consciousness is called the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).
The treatise states:
"In this way, it proceeds accordingly," and so on, up to the detailed exposition.
This citation serves as proof;
the latter explanation is correct,
as all treatises agree.
The *Nyāyānusāra* previously stated that consciousness is named after its sense organ (*indriya*).
Having finished establishing this as correct, it says:
"Some say..."
Those [objects] are the objective spheres (viṣaya) and not the sense organs (indriya).
However, because there is no consciousness that takes color-form (rūpa) and so forth as its object, it is called "consciousness of color-form" (rūpādi-vijñāna).
It is a fault to claim that the basis of that consciousness is the eye and so forth.
Because it is distinguished by the term "pure matter" (*rūpa-prasāda*),
the commentary explains that the phrase "the pure matter which is the basis" excludes the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*).
The mental consciousness has as its support non-material form (*arūpa-rūpa*). Furthermore, it says: "If that were so..."
The mention of "form" (rūpa) would then be redundant, because the meaning—
that those consciousnesses depend on the pure bases known as the eye-faculties and so forth—
is already established.
It is not the support for consciousness;
it is pure and non-material (*arūpa*).
To distinguish it from that [consciousness], the term "material" (*rūpa*) should be employed. Commentary:
This is difficult.
If you claim that "pure matter" (viśuddha-rūpa) serves to distinguish it from the mental faculty (manas-indriya),
then it should simply be "pure."
Without relying on the term "form," there are two kinds of purity among all phenomena.
The first is the five sense faculties.
The second refers to faith (*śraddhā*).
Faith is a mental factor (*caitasika*) and is not the basis for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The five faculties are material (*rūpa*) and are not the faculty of mind (*manendriya*).
If one were to say simply that "that consciousness relies on the pure," this would already exclude the mental faculty (*manas*);
therefore, to further add the word "matter" (*rūpa*) would be redundant. Such is the explanation.
The term "form" (rūpa) must be included in order to dispel doubts and difficulties.
If the term "consciousness-support" (vijñānāśraya) were analyzed according to the possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*),
then pure faith (*śraddhā*) would have to be called an eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) and so forth.
Therefore, the term "form" (rūpa) is set aside to exclude this interpretation;
there is not a single dharma that takes consciousness as its support.
One may provide this explanation: "Form is pure.
Therefore, the term "form" is extremely useful. The commentary states:
To speak directly, that consciousness relies upon purity;
if analyzed according to the *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) compound,
"faith" is termed the support of consciousness.
Because it relies on consciousness through faith, there is a consciousness that has a basis;
taking the name of that consciousness, it is called "relying on consciousness.
Its essence, moreover, is pure.
If one were to state directly that "that consciousness relies on purity" without including the term "form," it would lead to the ambiguity of a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound.
Faith is called the support for consciousness;
furthermore, it is its purification.
Thus, pure faith itself should be designated as the faculties, such as the eye and so forth.
If the term "form" (rūpa) were omitted, this explanation would not be confused [with other cases].
Formlessness (ārūpya) is pure;
it takes consciousness as its support.

Since it is explained as a possessive compound (bahuvrīhi) meaning "that which has the support of consciousness," the inclusion of the word *rūpa* (form) is extremely useful. Some people, failing to grasp this point, claim that the three terms—
*vijñāna-āśraya-viśuddha* (the pure support of consciousness)— are mutually contradictory when interpreted as a possessive compound.
It says: "To claim there is the 'ekadeśa-ubhaya-bhāgīya' (partial-both-part) interpretation is an error. It further says:
"Moreover, regarding what was previously stated herein..."
This is to exclude the four faculties, such as the ear;
for although they all have pure matter (*rūpaprasāda*) as their nature,
they do not serve as the support for visual consciousness.
Therefore, those four faculties are not subsumed under the eye faculty.
The subsequent statement is intended to distinguish them from the support that has ceased without interval.
Although that [mind-base] also serves as the support for visual consciousness, it does not have pure matter as its intrinsic nature;
therefore, that mental faculty is not subsumed under the visual faculty. Alternatively, as stated previously:
The preceding statement reveals the eye that possesses a commonality (sabhāga);
the subsequent statement is for the purpose of revealing the eye that does not possess a commonality (tatsabhāga).
The same applies to the other faculties. The commentary states:
As previously mentioned, this is the support for visual consciousness.
The latter says:
"This is pure matter (rūpa). It further states:
"If that were so, since the characteristics of pure matter would not differ, the five [senses] should not be established."
Not so; for there is a distinction in their functional capacities (*śakti*).
How is it known that these capacities are distinct?
Regarding the consciousness that does not share its object, because its basis is fixed;

and so forth, as explained at length. The Sarvāstivādins and others maintain that the five faculties have translucent matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) as their essence; the Mahāsāṃghikas maintain that the five faculties have a mass of flesh as their essence; and Buddhadēva maintains that they have the four great elements as their essence. Having already discussed the five faculties, the treatise now discusses the five objects.
The third verse clarifies the five sense objects.
Within the verse, flavor (*rasa*) is mentioned first and fragrance (*gandha*) second.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"The reason for explaining them out of order is to demonstrate that there is no fixed sequence in the arising of consciousnesses with respect to their respective objects."
Since the treatise provides this explanation, we know that "sound" and "fragrance" are not treated as transgressions [in this context], and that fragrance follows taste.
The treatise says: "Up to the differentiation of the four types of form."
This explains the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
Within this, there are six sections;
the five sense objects constitute five of these sections.

The sixth [section] concerns the general and specific classifications of the consciousnesses that arise. Regarding the specific explanation of the objective sphere of form (*rūpa-āyatana*), there are three parts:
first, the explanation of the two types of form;
second, the opening of the twenty types of form.
The analysis of the third and fourth lines constitutes the first explanation of the two types of form (*rūpa*). Regarding the "two types of form":
the first is visible (*sanidarśana*).
The two genders.
This explanation clarifies the primary colors (*varṇa*). Regarding the four primary colors, there are the fundamental primary colors.
These are blue, yellow, red, and white.
Other manifest colors that are differentiations of these four are:
cloud, smoke, dust, mist, shadow, glare, light, and darkness.
These eight types of color, according to their respective natures, are the distinctions of colors such as blue, yellow, and so forth:

that which arises from the breath of dragons and the like is called "cloud"; that which arises from fire is called "smoke"; that which is dispersed in fragments is called "dust"; the vapor of the earth is called "mist"; that which arises from the sun is called "light"; that which arises from jewels, the moon, and so forth is called "radiance"; when light or radiance is obstructed and other objects become visible therein, it is called "shadow"; the opposite of this is called "darkness. Although these eight distinctions differ, [they are all forms].
The fundamental [colors] are blue and so forth;
there are also variations such as azure, red, purple, and green.
These differ in terms of lightness and depth.
There is a difference between separation and combination;
they are not established as distinct categories.
What is a light blue is called "bi" (azure).
A slight red is called crimson;
blue and yellow combined form green;
red and black combined form purple.
Treatise:
There are eight types of shape (saṃsthāna), from long to uneven as the last;
this enumerates the shapes. The *Nyāyānusāra* says:
Among these, there are twelve kinds of color-forms (varṇa) and eight kinds of shape-forms (saṃsthāna).
Their names are as follows:
Treatise:
Alternatively, there are twenty [elements], extending from the shadow, light, and darkness;
this second classification divides the two types of matter into twenty.
Treatise:
Other masters say it extends to the twenty-first [moment].
This describes a divergent opinion; the intention of this master is as follows:
The single visible color of space is neither light nor darkness;
it is established as a distinct color, thus making twenty-one.
According to the correct tenet of the *Vibhāṣā*, the single visible color of space is a portion of the color of the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).
The form of the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*) is precisely the forms of light, darkness, and so forth;
it has no separate intrinsic nature.
Nevertheless, light, darkness, and the like—
It is established based on the distinctions of the four colors, such as blue and so forth.
Therefore, the *Vijñānakāya-pāda-śāstra*, fascicle eleven, states:
"The color of space is a single manifestation."
Regarding "such as blue, yellow, and so forth":
this is established based on the distinctions of blue and the like; or it refers to colors that resemble the distinctions of blue and so forth, yet are not identical to blue and the like.
Therefore, it is called "suchness" (tathatā). Regarding this treatise,
as for the term "correct" (zhèng), since it has already been fully explained, it will not be further commented upon here.
This is to resolve the difficulties regarding form and color (*rūpa*).
Regarding these characteristics of form and color, many masters of the past and present have failed to grasp their true meaning;
they have not relied upon the sacred teachings but have instead described their characteristics erroneously. Now, I shall clarify these characteristics through a twofold analysis.
First, the exposition of the correct meaning;
second, the narration of divergent views and their refutations. Regarding the exposition of the correct meaning:
this concerns the treatises of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
This describes the eight types of color-form (*rūpa*).
In all of them, length and shortness are established without mutual dependence.
*Mahāyānasaṃgraha-karmasiddhi-śāstra*.
Regarding the Sarvāstivāda and other schools,
they establish eight material characteristics;
furthermore, in this treatise’s Karma-pāda, the Sautrāntika establishes these eight material characteristics against the Sarvāstivāda.
All say: when the faces meet evenly, one arises in perfect enlightenment;
when the faces meet unevenly, one arises in imperfect enlightenment.
When one sees that one side is large, the perception of "long" arises;
when one sees that one side is small, the perception of "short" arises; when one sees all four sides as equal, the perception of "square" arises;
and when one sees it produced in all directions, the perception of "round" arises.
Seeing that which is convex in the center, one gives rise to the perception of height;
seeing that which is concave in the center, one gives rise to the perception of depth. Although there are slight differences between the two treatises, their general meaning is the same.
According to this scriptural authority:
The two colors, long and short, do not exist by being established through mutual dependence;
rather, they are each distinct entities and aspects.
According to the system established in the treatises, their respective characteristics differ. This is the explanation according to the Mahāyāna.
This means that according to the Sarvāstivāda interpretation, "long," "short," and so forth are names for the different arrangements of manifest colors (*varṇa*).

There exists a distinct subtle form (*rūpa-paramāṇu*) that sustains these eight types of characteristics. Since ancient times, teachers of both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna have been confused by this, mistakenly identifying a single surface with multiple [dimensions] as being "long."
On one hand, some offer brief and superficial explanations,
providing various interpretations,
yet none of them capture the true meaning.
Thus, it is said that [the designations] such as "long" are established through mutual dependence. Now, this is explained:
"one side has many [atoms]" means that among the six sides, one side has many [atoms].
It should also be among the six sides; however,
as two sides would predominate,
it is feared that this might be difficult to understand.
Therefore, it is said to have "one side.
For example, bamboo, bamboo shoots, and melons are called "long-colored" (dīrghavarṇa).
If one says there are many [sides], then there would be two sides.
People do not understand which two faces are among the six faces;
therefore, it is said that one face is many and one face is few.
As for "one face being few":
By reversing this, it can be understood that "long" is the subtle and "short" is the coarse.
Therefore, among the eight types of matter (*rūpa*), coarse and subtle are not established as distinct categories. This is stated in the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Chapter on Karma (*Karmavarga*).
It is said that apart from manifest color, there exists a distinct subtle shape which is the object of visual consciousness,
and which is accumulated as length and so forth.
This is conventional and not real;
it is an object of the mental consciousness alone, not the domain of visual consciousness.
This conventional length and so forth exist only because they are sustained by the boundaries of shape (*saṃsthāna*).
Other objects may enter within it,
breaking apart its distinct components;
the interior may be perforated to form holes and cavities, and so forth.
Only then does it possess shape and color.
The intent of the treatise is merely to state that, apart from the manifest [color], there exists a distinct subtle form.
It is not said that there are eight types of subtle forms;
their essential natures are inherently distinct. Now, upon careful examination, there are two kinds of shape-color (saṃsthāna-rūpa), such as length and so forth.
First, they receive their names through mutual dependence.
Second, because their forms and dimensions are each distinct, their names are established based on such mutual dependence;
for their substance is not fixed.
In this context, the distinct shapes and dimensions are not explained, because their essential natures (*svabhāva*) are different;
this is what is being discussed here. The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle nine, states:
"The five [aggregates] exist in mutual dependence."
That is to say, matters such as "this shore" and "the other shore," or "long" and "short," do not constitute distinct categories within the essence of luminous form (*rūpa*),
because such matters as length and shortness apply to other phenomena as well.
Even if one speaks of form (*rūpa*), it does not contradict this,
because these are previously included under the designation of "mutual dependence" (*apekṣā*). Furthermore, with respect to their distinct shapes and dimensions,
there are two categories.
First, external conditions arise,
such as gold or stone,
which require craftsmen and other factors to grow and develop; second, their natures are distinct.
Just as the nature of salt is square,
for even after it has been scattered and dissolved into water, it returns to its square shape;
likewise, the yuegua gourd grows naturally [into that shape].
The melon is short by nature;
the walnut varies in height;
the cherry is naturally round.
The nature of the bean is perverse;
such things as these differ according to their respective categories.
If they were established only by depending on conditions, [they would lack intrinsic nature].
If categorized by their types,
none of these are names established through mutual dependence;
for example, although a needle is short in relation to a gourd, [it is not so in relation to other objects].
This is the color of length.
Although the melon is long in relation to the jujube,
it is the color of shortness.
All of these are produced as long, short, and so forth by the respective powers of long and short atoms;
yet the atoms of length and shortness do not intermingle.
Furthermore, for this very reason, length and so forth are not established in other objects;
there are no distinct shape-atoms that cause a simultaneous aggregation to become long and so forth. The rest of the text is easy to understand.
Therefore, it is not explained here. Regarding the presentation of divergent views:
some say that "long" and "short" [refer to...]
Long and short atoms each possess their own distinct substance;
they abide in mutual intermingling,
such that what is long in shape appears as short.
To explain the short while seeing the long, [the critic] rebuts: "This interpretation violates both the teaching and the principle.
As for violating the teaching:
upon what sutra or śāstra do you rely to make such an interpretation?"
This contradicts the *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa* and this very treatise;
furthermore, when multiple names refer to the same entity, it is designated as "long."
Regarding the point that "a single side is slightly named 'short' when it contradicts reason":
within a single material form (*rūpa*), there exist both long and short atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Although its shape is long, it is perceived as short.
Just as one who is short in stature does not see those who are tall, so too,
one who lacks length does not see those who are short.
If there is no short, one does not see the long. If that were so,
then the long and the short would exist simultaneously, defined in relation to one another.
One should perceive length by means of shortness;
yet when there is no occasion for length and shortness to be defined in relation to one another,
one does not perceive the two colors of long and short according to objects.
When one attends directly to what is before one's eyes and perceives long or short forms,
why are they not seen?
It must wait for comparison with other forms.
All of these are unreasonable.
Furthermore, since it is known by depending on comparison,
it is an object of the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) and not something grasped by the visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna).
Since visual consciousness cannot perform mental calculation regarding its objects, it is known to be unreasonable. Furthermore,
the claim that "that which can be measured is called long,
and that which cannot be measured is called short" also contradicts both scripture and reason.
Furthermore, there is contradiction with the world and contradiction with the teachings.
Regarding contradiction with the teachings, as cited previously; regarding contradiction with reason:
As stated regarding the sense-object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*), that which cannot be weighed is called light,
while that which can be weighed is called heavy;
this does not distinguish between quantity.
If merely pulling down a scale is called "heavy contact," then this case should also be so:
if there is merely a dimension, it should be called "long."
That which consists of seven or more atoms possesses magnitude and should be called "long.
In the world, there is no such thing as perceiving a short color [that lacks this magnitude]. To contradict worldly convention:
no one in the entire world refers to that which can be measured as being "long."
"Immeasurable" means "short. Furthermore, it asks and answers its own question:
"Since these short atoms are numerous, how can they be said to be immeasurable? The explanation says:
Although it possesses multiple entities,
it cannot be measured;
just as a subtle atom (paramāṇu), though possessing multiple entities, is immeasurable.
They are beyond measure;
though short and minute,
they are too numerous to be reckoned.
If it is said that what is seen by the eye is not immeasurable,
then since visibility is also seen by the eye,
it too should be measurable.
If it is argued that what is gathered together in the same collection should be measurable,
then fragrance and so forth, being gathered in the same collection,
should likewise be measurable.
Since these are mixed together and cannot be measured,
and since short and long are likewise mixed and cannot be measured, there is, according to the explanation above,
no logical basis whatsoever for this.
The preceding and succeeding [statements] contradict one another.
According to the above, the thesis was established and the distinctions between long and short forms were explained;
the second explanation states:
That which can be measured and has already passed away is called "long form"; that is to say,
a measurable aggregate of matter is termed "long," while an immeasurable aggregate is termed "short form."
The resolution of the objection states that short atoms and long atoms abide in mutual intermingling. According to this principle, that which is already measurable is both long and short;
even an immeasurable aggregate is both short and long.
Is this not in direct contradiction with your own tenet? Furthermore, the analogy cited regarding tangibility is also illogical;
the essential nature of atoms is not necessarily heavy.
Therefore, a single atom of tangibility cannot move a scale;
nor is a multitude of them heavy.
Since the substance of the seven atoms is a phenomenon characterized by resistance (*sapratigha*), a multitude of them must necessarily be measurable.
How is this established as a precedent? Furthermore, he himself explains the characteristics of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), stating:
"That which is convex in the center is called 'high' (*unnata*); that which is concave in the center is called 'low' (*avanata*)."
The self-interrogation and response states:
"What is the difference between long and high?
What is the distinction between short and low?"
The author’s own commentary states:
"Length and shortness are determined by the horizontal;
height and depth are determined by the vertical. According to this, the preceding [definitions] would contradict themselves.
How could it be that what is convex vertically is called "high," what is convex horizontally is called "long," and what is concave vertically is called "low"?
That which is horizontally concave is called "short. Furthermore, all Mahāyāna masters state that the manifestation of an aggregation constitutes "long" and so forth;
they further explain that "long" and the rest are established through mutual dependence.
Clear comprehension (*abhijñā*) refers precisely to the provisional aggregation of length and so forth;
this is exclusively an object-condition for the mental consciousness (*manas*).

What is the sense-field of form? Furthermore, how could an aggregate of touch and so forth lack length? [The Treatise says: The sense-field of form refers to that which is visible and possesses resistance. It is of two kinds: color-form (*varṇa-rūpa*) and shape-form (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*). Color-form consists of blue, yellow, red, white, cloud, smoke, dust, mist, shadow, glare, light, and darkness. Shape-form consists of long, short, square, round, high, low, even, uneven, coarse, and fine. As for the question of how an aggregate of touch and so forth could lack length: since the atoms of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*) arise in conjunction with one another, they necessarily occupy spatial extension. Therefore, when these atoms aggregate, they manifest as long, short, and so on; it is not the case that they lack such dimensions. Thus, even though the individual atoms themselves may not possess the conventional designations of "long" and so forth, their aggregation does indeed result in the manifestation of such shapes. This is because the spatial arrangement of the constituent parts constitutes the basis for the perception of length and other such forms. Consequently, there is no contradiction in asserting that aggregates of touch and the like possess length.
There are some visible objects that extend into shadow, light, or darkness.
This is analyzed in the third and fourth propositions.
Now, in order to explain these four propositions, one must understand shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*). Herein lies the detailed examination.
There are three different types of form and magnitude.
The first refers to extremely obstructive aggregates that arise without depending on anything else for support.
The second [category] consists of those that possess their own shape and dimensions and do not depend upon anything else,
such as walls, trees, and so forth;
these may be pierced or hollowed out to form cavities and the like.
Like clouds, smoke, and so forth—
these three depend on others for their establishment as valid cognitions and are incapable of being shaken.
It is like light, luminosity, and so forth, as well as paintings and the like.
Some say that a painting possesses shape, but this is an error; most treatises take the first type of shape (saṃsthāna-rūpa) as "shape."
One may take the second, or one may take the third.
The eight types of shape mentioned in the preceding text constitute the first; here, the four propositions include the second type of shape as well.

Because clouds, smoke, and so forth are included within the category of both [color and shape], there may be instances where a locus of color possesses manifest color (varṇa) but lacks shape (saṃsthāna).
This refers to manifest color that does not coexist with a shape.
That is to say, excluding the twelve [colors] that are both manifest and shaped, all others— which are manifest but not shaped,
such as blue and so forth— are exclusively manifest color (*varṇa*). The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise on Following Reasoning), fascicle 34, states:
Alternatively, there are material aggregates where both [shape and color] are perceivable;
that is to say, the remaining aggregates of shape and color.
This is because, in these aggregates, one cannot perceive the other apart from the first. Based on this, it should be understood.
It does not coalesce with form;
this name reveals that it is not form.
Treatise.
Alternatively, there are instances where the sense-base of form reaches the nature of bodily informative action;
this is the second alternative.
It refers to the form of bodily informative action.
Although at the time of its arising it is gathered together with the old continuum of visible form (*varṇa*),
it does not necessarily coexist with it.
It is because its initial arising and its cessation are distinct from its manifestation.
When first arising, there is no new visible form (*varṇa*);
when ceasing, it is because the continuity of the ancient visible form persists. As the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
The principle that what is called bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) is a particularity of shape (*saṃsthāna-viśeṣa*) is fully established. That is to say,

it is a distinct category of visible form (*rūpa*) produced from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that are non-abiding and not of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*), which arise from the mind of preparatory effort (*prayoga-citta*).
Without depending on other visible colors as the cause for the arising of visual consciousness,
it can obscure the shape produced by maturation (vipākaja) that is nurtured by food;
such a shape is called bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti).
Treatise:
Or, there are bases of form that reach what is called "the remaining forms";
this is the third phrase.
This refers to the visible matter (rūpa) that is co-existent with shape (saṃsthāna).
As previously cited from the *Nyāyānusāra*, the treatise states: [text].
Other masters say that it exists because length and so forth reach [the object].
This describes a divergent opinion; this master also includes the third shape, while only a portion of the color of light lacks shape.
This refers to the radiance emitted from that which is unobstructed;
because its color gradually fades, it has no fixed dimensions. Some say this refers to newly arisen wisdom, but that is incorrect.
Treatise:
How can a single entity possess both color (varṇa) and shape (saṃsthāna)?
This is the objection from the Sautrāntika school. The intent of the objection is as follows:
The sense-sphere of form, such as length and so forth, is precisely color (varṇa) and shape (saṃsthāna).
These distinct names are established based on the state of aggregation.
How can a single atom (paramāṇu) be both color and shape?
Treatise:

Because within this context it reaches the meaning of "non-existence of the object," the Master [Vasubandhu] answers according to the intention of the Sautrāntikas. Herein, it is actually a single form that gives rise to two cognitions: those of color and shape.

The first six are the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness.
The first four elements are subsumed within the element of tangibility (spraṣṭavyadhātu).
The space element has light, shadow, brightness, and darkness as its essence;
it is comprised within the aggregate of form.
The consciousness element has contaminated consciousness as its essence.
The seven mind-elements include the second group of six, namely:

the element of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the element of ill-will (*vyāpādadhātu*), the element of cruelty (*vihiṃsādhātu*), the element of non-desire (*akāmadhātu*), the element of non-ill-will (*avyāpādadhātu*), and the element of non-cruelty (*avihiṃsādhātu*).
Desire has sensual craving as its intrinsic nature; ill-will has hatred as its intrinsic nature.
Harmfulness has harm as its intrinsic nature;
non-desire has non-greed as its intrinsic nature;
and non-ill will has non-hatred as its intrinsic nature.
Non-harming has non-injury as its intrinsic nature.

These six are mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) and are all subsumed within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*). The third group of six consists of the elements of pleasure, pain, joy, sorrow, equanimity, and ignorance.
The first five realms have sensation as their intrinsic nature;
the last one has delusion as its intrinsic nature,
because it is a mental factor (*caitta-dharma*).
All are subsumed within the dharma-dhātu. First, there are four types:
the elements of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are subsumed within the element of phenomena (dharma-dhātu).
The consciousness element is subsumed within the seven mind-elements. Third, there are six types.
The first three are the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
The desire realm is comprised of the eighteen elements (dhātus).
The form realm (rūpadhātu) is comprised of fourteen elements (dhātu),
excluding the two [elements] of odor and taste,
as well as the consciousnesses of the nose and tongue.
The mind, mental objects, and mind-consciousness elements of the formless realm are subsumed [within the consciousness element]. Second are the three realms:
namely, the realm of form, the formless realm, and the cessation realm.
The realm of form refers to the desire realm and the form realm.
Because they possess form, they are collectively termed the Form Realm (rūpadhātu).
They are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus).
The Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu) is subsumed within the final three elements.
The realm of cessation has the nature of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
It is subsumed within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The third [set of] three realms refers to the past and the future.
The present realm has the five aggregates as its nature and is subsumed within the eighteen realms.
This is the fourth of the three realms.
That is to say, there are the inferior, intermediate, and superior realms.
The inferior realm has unwholesome and obscured-neutral phenomena as its nature;
it is subsumed within the seven mind-elements, the element of form, the element of sound, and the element of mental objects.
The intermediate realm has as its nature tainted wholesome phenomena and non-obscured neutral phenomena;
it is comprised within the eighteen realms.
The sublime realm has as its nature untainted wholesome phenomena.
The fifth set of three realms consists of the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
These are the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate realms.
The wholesome realm has all wholesome phenomena as its intrinsic nature.
The unwholesome element has all unwholesome phenomena as its nature;
these two [elements] are subsumed within the seven mental elements, the elements of visible form, sound, and mental objects.
The indeterminate element has all indeterminate phenomena as its nature.

Inclusion within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*): the sixth consists of three elements, namely, the element of those in training (*śaikṣa*), the element of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and the element of those who are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
The element of those in training has as its nature the five untainted (*anāsrava*) aggregates (*skandha*) of one in training.
The *aśaikṣa-dhātu* (the realm of those beyond training) has as its nature the five untainted (*anāsrava*) aggregates of one beyond training.
These two [realms] are subsumed within the mental faculty (*manas*), the mental object (*dharma*), and the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) elements.
This is the realm that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣa-nāśaikṣa-dhātu*).
It has as its nature the five contaminated aggregates (*skandha*) and the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
It is subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*). Regarding the "last two" and "the second":
the first refers to the first two elements.
This refers to the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) realms.
The contaminated realm has the five contaminated aggregates as its nature and is subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
The untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) refers to the five untainted aggregates (*skandha*), as well as the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*);
it is comprised within the mental faculty (*manas*), the mental object (*dharma*), and the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) realms—namely, the second two realms.
These are the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) realms.
The conditioned realm (saṃskṛta-dhātu) has the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) as its nature and is subsumed within the eighteen realms (aṣṭādaśa-dhātu).
The unconditioned realm (asaṃskṛta-dhātu) has the three unconditioned phenomena (trīṇy asaṃskṛtāni) as its nature.
Included in the *Dharmadhātu*: The *Āgama* scriptures also enumerate the names of sixty-two elements (*dhātu*), titled the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra*.
May you understand this and enjoy long life.
